Press Release:


Trade In Exotic Pets
Exotic animals like arctic foxes, monkeys and snakes make popular suburban pets. Some of these rare animals fetch big bucks in the trade, making breeding, importation and wild capture a lucrative business. But who pays the ultimate price? Carte Blanche investigates the pet shops and breeders who keep this multi-million rand industry alive.


Script:


In South Africa buying and owning an exotic pet from a shark to an arctic fox is perfectly legal. Yet the trade of these animals remains dogged in controversy.
LINK: So where do you buy an exotic pet? Online through a breeder or at a pet shop, but once you make that decision do you fully understand your responsibilities.
Dee Hendricks runs an exotic parrot rescue centre called Brainy Birds in Edenvale.
Dee: “It actually started when I was 14 years old. I used to go home passed the pet shop, and saw this little bird in a terrible condition stuck in a cage. So I pinched it.”
Dee says the majority of the birds she helps are pets who are no longer a novelty to their owners.
“This bird doesn’t understand it because he’s bonded to you. Now he’s biting me, he’s biting the children, he’s plucking his feathers out. I don’t want the bird.”
Dee: “I don’t think exotic pets, especially exotic pets that live for 70 years, should be kept in captivity.”
Arno: “The trade in exotics is massive in South Africa, although most people don’t know about it, because a lot of it is kept very quiet."
Vice Chairman of the South African Pet Traders Association Arno Naude has 42 years of experience as a reptile breeder. He says traders can make big bucks on exotics like fish, reptiles and EVEN insects.
Arno: “They breed these specifically as a pet, because somebody living in a flat who can’t have a dog, or a cat or are allergic to it, and they want to keep something to nurture, they don’t mind keeping something like a small little stick insect and feeding it rose leaves.”
Arno says the laws around the sale and ownership of exotic pets aren’t working.
Arno: “In places like Krugersdorp you can’t even keep a spider, you have to ask the chief of the fire department for permission to keep a spider. Now that’s ridiculous. We need to get rules that work for the pet and for the person.”
We visited a number of pet stores around Gauteng. One of them was West Rand Pet and Bird Farm in Roodepoort. These photos taken in 2013 lead the NSPCA to investigate this business. Head of the NSPCA’s animal protection unit, Ainsley Hay, says some reptiles bones had disintegrated from metabolic bone disease.
Ainsley: “If you keep a reptile very cold, their metabolism shuts down which creates very brittle bones and they’ll get multiple fractures.”
Glen Hatfield owns West Rand Pet and Bird Farm. He says he loves animals and disputes the NSPCA’s findings.
Glen: “No charges were ever formally placed against the bird farm. We’ve never seen that report, we did ask for the opportunity for someone to examine them, and we’ve never been given that opportunity.”
Glen says the Roodepoort SPCA now conducts regular inspections at his premises and they have found no further problems.
This arctic fox – snowy - was for sale in 2013. In the wild these animals live in extremely cold conditions, burrow and have territories spanning kilometres.
Glen: “Because we haven’t got a zoo license to actually display animals, they have to be seen as being for sale.”
Devi: “You took advantage of a loophole?”
Glen: “Yes”
Devi: “But why are you admitting that to me?”
Glen: “Because that’s the rules, I say the animal was never for sale.”
Leon Lotter from the Gauteng Department of Nature Conservation explains that West Rand Pet and Bird Farm only needed the zoo license when they had indigenous animals, which they no longer have.
Leon: “Historically zoo permits were issued much easier, but now we have clamped down on that.”
Two years later we visited snowy, living in the same cage with a concrete floor. He’s now part of a petting zoo.
Glen: The reason why there’s a concrete floor is because they tend to dig.
Devi: But that’s their natural behaviour?
Glen: I think it’s adequate, obviously you can always give animals bigger cages.”
Government has plans to institute minimum cage requirements in zoos, for example, arctic foxes would need a 50 square meter cage, per pair.
Pay R5 and you can feed the monkeys coloured popcorn.
Glen: “Those would be treats, that’s not the daily diet that we give them.”
But the law does not regulate a captive animals diet.
This High Fin or Paroon shark is a critically endangered giant cat fish – on sale for R1,500 rand. In the wild they live in rivers and can grow up to 3m long and weigh 300Kg’s, however, Glen says in captivity it will not grow to that size.
Glen: “ for now, the size of the tank is okay.”
Arno says the industry needs solutions.
“We should look at system where a person is actually taught, educated, writes an exam, and he’s licensed to keep the animal.”
Arno says permits aren’t preventative.
“A tiger with a permit can still jump over the fence and eat the child next door, if the owner has a license, he has specific requirements he needs to meet.”
At Exotic in Boksburg – an exotic pet store specializing in fish, we saw that for R23,000 you can buy a black tip reef shark. Although these can be caught locally, which would require a permit, this one was not. A pet shop employee explains.
Pet shop employee: “You get them local as well, but then you need permits for them.
Journalist: Oh. I see. Okay so this is?
Pet shop employee: from Indonesia, it’s imported, we’ve the papers for the importation. ”
In a written response owner of exotic, Adam Scott, says this shark was legally imported and is very happy swimming in its tank, however, they are building one three times bigger. He said he doesn’t believe in sharks as pets, but rather educational displays for people who never get to see them in the wild. However, he doesn’t think it’s cruel to keep them as pets should someone wish to buy this one.
Across the road from Exotic is Loolilocks – they specialize is Koi, but have a variety of other animals.
Like this Caymen.
And these lemer’s.
Another Arctic fox, whose nails can be heard on the concrete floor.
This blue and gold macaw doesn’t seem to fit into its cage.
In a dark room we found tenerics, jars of arachnids and reptiles, like snakes and iguana’s.
LINK: We wrote 3 emails to Loolilocks. No response. So we decided to pay them a visit in person.
They asked us to leave and call back later, after which the owner declined an interview.
Manager: “The reason being, there’s so much politics in the trade we just don’t want to be a part of it hey.”
Leon says breeders of exotics have asked for some regulation.
Leon: “So the department has developed a new nature conservation bill and the bill will regulate alien species in a better way.”
However, as there is currently no legislation when it comes to pet shops, nothing prevents someone from buying dangerous animals. When one Pretoria owner could no longer keep this python, they took extreme measures.
Arno: “They actually just killed it, and threw it in a dustbin next to the road, so that it could not be traced back to the people who actually had it.”
Good news for Snowy from West Rand Pet and Bird Farm.
Glen: “We’ve agreed to donate it.”
Glen says the Roodepoort SPCA has found him a climate controlled home, away from the public, at Butterfly world in Stellenbosch.
Glen: “Our trade, as such, is driven by the public, if people didn’t want to keep animals in their homes, we would be out of business. I don’t think it’s unethical to sell them, as long as that the people are given the correct advice, and obviously we sell animals that are healthy.”
Dee believes that making a profit from animals is unethical.
Dee: “Why do you think this bird looks like that? Because of money. Not love. This is a live thing, it has a feeling, it’s like me and you. Human. “
